title: Steamed Whole Sea Bass with Ginger, Spring Onions and Sizzling Oil
summary: Whole sea bass is steamed over ginger and spring onion until just cooked, then dressed with a savoury soy sauce and finished with a dramatic splash of sizzling hot oil.
equipment: wok with lid or a large steamer that fits a plate (at least 32 cm)
heatproof plate that fits inside with 2 cm to spare
foil sling (a long strip of folded foil under the plate)

ingredients.item: whole sea bass or bream, about 600 g each, scaled and gutted
ingredients.note: about 30 cm long, to fit your steamer

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt

ingredients.note: half sliced, half in fine matchsticks
whites in 5 cm lengths, greens in fine shreds

ingredients.item: light soy sauce (alcohol-free; check the label)

steps.title: Prepare the Fish
steps.text: Rinse the sea bass inside and out and pat them dry. Score three shallow diagonal cuts, about 1 cm deep, down each side of each fish, taking care not to cut through to the bone, then rub all over and inside with the salt. These cuts let heat reach the thickest part of the fish at the same rate as the thinner flesh, so everything finishes cooking together.

steps.title: Arrange on the Plate
steps.text: Lay the spring-onion whites and sliced ginger over the base of your steaming plate and set the fish on top, tucking a few more ginger slices into each cavity. Raising the fish off the plate this way lets steam circulate underneath as well as over the top, so it cooks evenly.

steps.title: Mix the Sauce
steps.text: Stir the soy sauce, sugar and hot water together until the sugar dissolves, then stir in the white pepper. Having the sauce ready before the fish goes in means you can dress it the moment it comes out of the steamer, while everything is still hot.

steps.title: Steam Until Just Cooked
steps.text: Pour about 5 cm of water into your wok, bring it to a rolling boil, then lower the plate onto the rack using a foil sling. Cover tightly and steam over high heat for 10-14 minutes, checking thicker fish first at 10 minutes, until the flesh next to the backbone is opaque, flakes easily and reaches at least 63°C. Keeping the water at a hard, steady boil throughout keeps the steam hot enough to cook the fish quickly, which is what keeps it moist rather than dry.

steps.title: Drain and Dress
steps.text: Carefully lift the plate out using the foil sling and oven gloves, as the steam underneath is fierce. Tip off the cloudy liquid that's collected on the plate and discard the ginger and spring onion from underneath and inside the fish, since they've given up their flavour and the liquid itself tastes rather fishy. Pour the prepared sauce around the fish and scatter over the ginger matchsticks, spring-onion greens and chilli.

steps.title: Sizzle the Oil
steps.text: Heat the oil in a small pan over high heat until just smoking, then carefully pour it straight over the ginger and spring onion on top of the fish. It will crackle loudly and release their aroma instantly; hot oil poured over raw aromatics cooks them in seconds and lifts their fragrance far more than steaming them with the fish from the start.

steps.title: Carve and Serve
steps.text: Scatter over the coriander and bring the fish to the table at once, while the oil is still gently sizzling. Lift the top fillets off the bone first, then remove the backbone to reach the fillets underneath, spooning the sauce over each portion as you serve.

tips: Score the fish before steaming so the thick part by the backbone cooks through at the same time as the thinner belly flesh.
A common mistake is steaming over a weak simmer; keep the water at a full rolling boil so the fish cooks quickly and stays moist.
Discard the liquid and aromatics that collect under the fish before saucing it — they carry a fishy taste you don't want in the finished dish.
Have the sauce and sizzling oil ready to go before the fish is done, since this dish is best served the moment it comes out of the steamer.
storage: This dish is really best eaten straight away while the oil is still sizzling. If you do have leftovers, flake the fish off the bone, cover and refrigerate for up to 1 day, and reheat gently until piping hot (74°C) before eating; it doesn't freeze well. Cool leftovers in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours (within 1 hour on a day above 32°C).
